To help you find a gift for yours, I went digging through our archives and some of our favorite retailers for ideas that are sure to help, delight, or just impress her — whether she’s achy, a gourmand, or someone who likes the finer things. Our deputy editor, Simone Kitchens, calls Fellow’s Carter mug “truly unleakable”; it even has a splash guard designed for bumpy car rides.

It’ll make cooking her famous rigatoni a whole lot easier, with no oven mitts required and a strainer included. “You can dump a box of spaghetti right in and it fits,” says artist Laurie Simmons.

entry.title: There Are a Bunch of New White Button-ups in Town
entry.summary: Button-ups are doing something different these days, and I want in.
entry.content:
I’ve spent more time admiring white button-ups and button-downs on others than ever finding any that look good on me. If I wear the classic style, it’s a massively oversized, thrifted men’s button-down — women’s shirts are usually too slim in the chest, bodice, and arms, or cut at an awkward crop on my longer torso. But over the last few months, I’ve noticed twists on collars, cuffs, buttons, and bibs. Button-ups are doing something different these days, and I want in. I tried three that caught my eye and rounded up more styles by two categories — the ones with tuxedo touches and the ones with nontraditional collars and buttons.

Button-ups have been all about bibs, wing-tip collars, and a French (or otherwise long or exaggerated) cuff since Mathieu Blazy’s SS26 Chanel debut featured a tuxedo-bibbed Charvet button-up.

I discovered this while working on my latest story, and it’s quickly become my favorite white button-up. The tunic length, wing tip collar, and French cuffs remind me of the Chanel shirt. I love the loose fit and clean, minimal look. I style my button-ups with a low cut for a more dramatic look, and with this one I’m able to create a sharp neckline or leave it unbuttoned around the torso for a different look. I think this would look especially nice with a black midi skirt and kitten heels.

I’ve spotted a bunch of other twists on collars, necklines, and buttons. To start, there’s an abundance of stand and funnel-esque collars. To take it one step further, some have hardly a collar at all (which I discovered are called band collars, nonetheless). Alternatively, if you’re bored with traditional buttons, try out asymmetrical placket placements and other inversions.

The off-center buttons and a collar you can button to your chin, or fold downward for a turtleneck-esque look, remind me of a vintage doctor’s coat. This $50 top was sold out in white at the time of testing. The cotton is on the thinner side, and it runs large (I’m wearing an XS).

I spotted this on the brand’s designer, Susan Woo, at a preview for her winter 2026 collection and was instantly taken with how crisp it looked. I hardly even noticed the button-up’s signature subversion: button-up sides finished with grosgrain ribbons and mother-of-pearl buttons. Portuguese poplin, which felt finer to the touch than any of the other tops I tried, makes it an investment. I would have sized up to a medium for a slightly longer fit.

If you like to see the innards of your gadgets (everyone loves transparent tech these days), these are the headphones for you — especially now that they’re 20 percent off ahead of Black Friday.

While most headphones feature a single-driver setup to avoid complications, Nothing put a lot of time and effort into designing a three-driver configuration that’s more like what you might see in a stereo speaker. The theory is that by using drivers to handle their respective frequency ranges, you get better balance and more detail overall. In practice, they sound so good you can sense the placement of every instrument in a live performance (at least on well-produced tracks), and Nothing’s equalizer settings give you a lot of control over the sound profile of your pair.

entry.title: The Very Best Pizza Ovens
entry.summary: Wood-fired, gas, and electric ovens for everyone from the beginner to the serious pizzaiolo
entry.content:
It’s entirely possible to make a good pizza in your conventional oven. But if you’ve been putting the effort into making your own dough and you want to re-create that crispy New York–style bottom or charred Neapolitan-inspired crust at home, then there’s really only one option — you’ll need a dedicated pizza oven that can reach higher temps than a standard oven and retains enough heat to make make a round of personal pies for your family or — if you’re brave enough and have the stamina — full-size pizzas to supply a backyard party.

I was bitten by the pizza-at-home bug about seven years ago, and it quickly turned into an obsession. Since then, I’ve made thousands of pizzas in dozens of ovens, including the wood-fired Fire Within trailer that we use to run our pizza food truck (yes, I got bitten so hard I turned it into a business).

For the past month, I’ve been testing the latest and greatest pizza ovens for the aspiring pizzaiolo, putting each one through its paces (making more than 100 pizzas in the process). And truth be told, they’ve all been great. I’ve had good results from every oven included in this list, even those that didn’t quite make a top pick.

When it comes to shopping for a pizza oven to use at home, you’ll need to take into account what fuel type you want to use. There are three main options: gas, wood, or electric.

Gas is the most common and is more forgiving for beginners. Wood is the most nostalgic, and many would argue the smoke gives you a better-tasting crust, but it has a steeper learning curve, and managing temperature becomes the focus instead of turning a pizza. Electric ovens plug into a standard outlet and allow for cooking indoors (they’re not weatherproof, and unlike gas and wood models, aren’t meant for outdoor installation, though you can use them outdoors in a pinch).

Some ovens, like the Gozney Dome XL (Gen 2) and the Ooni Karu 2 (with a gas-burner accessory), are capable of doing both gas and wood. Just keep in mind, the majority of ovens are limited to the fuel type you select at purchase.

Unlike commercial pizza ovens that are designed to cook multiple pizzas at the same time, most home cooks only need space for a single 10- to 12-inch pizza.

However, as is the case with our best pizza oven overall, the Ooni Koda 2 Pro, there are several options for pizza-makers who want to cook bigger pies (up to 16 inches in this case) or more than one at a time.

Outside of cooking a pizza, I’ve frequently used various pizza ovens to roast anything from fish and steak to veggies and fajitas — which is an added bonus of a larger oven.

I’ve found that when making pizza for dinner, part of the fun is having each person shape and top their own pizza, so don’t get too hung up on size — when you’re doing multiple personal pizzas,  a smaller oven can be more than enough.

But if you’re planning on hosting get-togethers or just want to make pizza as fast as possible, we suggest looking at one of the several larger oven options.

Along with what size pizza an oven can hold, it’s important to take the overall size and weight of the oven into account. Baking stones are heavy. Pizza ovens are often very heavy and difficult to move around, so you’ll want to consider where you’re going to keep the oven before clicking that buy button.

There are some lightweights, like Gozney’s Arc Lite, which weighs just over 25 pounds and is very easy to move around, and the designed-to-be-portable Tread, coming in at just under 30 pounds. Both electric ovens I tested are light enough to move around as needed and small enough to stay on your countertop.

But bigger ovens are a lot heavier and bulkier: The Ooni Koda 2 Pro weighs 66 pounds, and while it’s possible to move it around when needed, you’re likely going to want a dedicated space for it. Gozney’s Dome XL (Gen 2) is a staggering 161 pounds — that’s getting a permanent spot on your patio.

Nearly every household pizza-oven brand loves to tout how hot its ovens can get, with most claiming they can hit 950 degrees Fahrenheit. (That’s the temperature at which true Neapolitan-style pizzas are cooked.) But (as you may already know) it takes a lot of practice to cook a pizza at that high of a temperature without burning it — and having a way to assess the temperature takes some of the guesswork out of the process.

Some ovens have a temperature sensor that reads the ambient air temperature inside the oven; others have a sensor that reads the bottom of the baking stone. That means it’s going to lag behind the surface temp while the oven preheats — so while it’s a nice feature to have, it isn’t essential. Even if the oven has temperature probes, that won’t help with pizza (though some high-end models do, and those open the door to other uses, as we’ll get into below). Gozney’s Arc Lite is the only oven I tested that lacks any sort of temperature gauge. The omission is intentional and a cost-saving measure, which is fitting for a budget oven — but you’ll want to put aside cash for some kind of thermometer.

Whether your pizza oven has a built-in temperature gauge or not, I strongly recommend having a temperature gun on hand for every oven, as it’s the best way to ensure you’re launching a pizza at the temperature you want. (I’ve used more expensive models like Gozney’s and cheap ones like this; they all work.) You’ll quickly learn which temperature works best for you, your dough, and the pizza you’re making.

Some measurement features are aimed at maximizing the versatility of these ovens (they can do a lot more than pizza). On some of the Ooni and Gozney models that feature a digital temperature gauge — like the Koda 2 Pro and Dome XL (Gen 2) — you can plug a temperature probe (or two) into the gauge and it’ll display the internal temperature of a steak, for example.

Ooni’s Koda 2 Max and Koda 2 Pro come with the Ooni Connect Digital Temperature Hub. That’s a Bluetooth transmitter that you can pair with the Ooni app on your phone, allowing you to monitor the oven’s temperature, the temperature of any food probes, and set timers (these are just reminders for you, however — you can’t set the flame to turn off automatically).

Fuel type: Gas | Cooking area: 1 16-inch pizza | Stone thickness: 20 mm | Temperature gauge: Digital, food probe support, Bluetooth monitoring | Dimensions: 26.9 x 25.7 x 15.5 inches | Weight: 66 pounds

I wasn’t sure what to expect from Ooni’s Koda 2 Pro, but it surprised me almost every step along the way. Its ample cooking surface has enough space for multiple pizzas or a single 16-inch pizza, and it retains heat really well. It also has Ooni’s Connect Digital Temperature Hub with Bluetooth connectivity for remote monitoring — all for just under $800. That’s a heck of a deal.

The Koda 2 Pro is big but not overwhelming. It weighs 66 pounds, meaning that while you’re most likely going to want to leave it in one place, it’s movable without too much effort if you need to use it in a different position in your yard.

The Koda 2 Pro uses Ooni’s G2 Gas technology that tapers the flames from the base of the burner to the roof of the oven on both sides. The end result, according to Ooni, is more even heat distribution. And I concur: The heat distribution was pretty equal across the stone.

After 20 minutes of preheat time, the stone’s temperature read between 660 and 700 degrees with an infrared temperature gun. I was a bit puzzled my first couple of times using the Koda 2 Pro because the onboard digital temp gauge read 350 degrees and I couldn’t get it to go much higher than that. It wasn’t until I paired the Ooni app on my iPhone with the digital hub that the temperature reading matched what I was seeing with my temp gun.

I asked Ooni about this and was told that the hub doesn’t come from the factory linked to a specific model of oven. Part of the initial pairing process asks you to pick your model, which in turn calibrates the hub to read the correct temperature. It’s an extra step I’m not entirely sure should be needed, but it takes just a few seconds to go through. After that initial pairing, I haven’t had issues with the temp reading.

The first pizza I launched into the Koda 2 Pro came out with a bottom that was baked but lacked any sort of color. The usual 20-minute preheat I used to keep tests consistent wasn’t enough to fully saturate the stone, and in turn it simply wasn’t hot enough. The 20-mm. thick stone takes more time to heat, and I just wasn’t patient enough. Once I gave the stone more time to soak up the heat, I started seeing better results, and the Koda 2 Pro didn’t really slow down.

In the Ooni app, you’re able to see the ambient temp of the oven and start and monitor a timer, or if you have a food probe plugged in, you can remotely check on the temperature of a steak or another type of meat you’re cooking in the Koda 2 Pro. Remote monitoring isn’t necessary, but it’s a quality-of-life feature that’s nice to have, especially if you’re moving between prepping in your kitchen indoors and the oven on a back patio.

The Koda 2 Pro is hard to beat at this price, especially when you take its overall size and capabilities into account. It’s an oven I’d have no issues recommending to my closest friends and family members.

Fuel type: Gas | Cooking area: 1 12-inch pizza | Stone thickness: 12 mm | Temperature gauge: None | Dimensions: 18.9 x 26.9 x 11.7 inches | Weight: 26.4 pounds

Gozney’s Arc Lite is downright cute. It’s ideal for beginners or those who don’t want to spend a lot, while its small design makes it easy to move around if you don’t have a dedicated space for a pizza oven, without giving up a lot in terms of overall functionality.

The Arc Lite looks similar to the rest of the bigger, more expensive Arc lineup. Gozney removed some features in order to hit the $399 price point, with the most notable omission being a temperature gauge of any kind. Instead of the digital display the Arc and Arc XL feature, the Arc Lite has a single dial used to ignite and control the flame inside the oven. In order to monitor the temp, you’ll want to use a handheld infrared thermometer. It’ll handle a 12-inch pizza with no issues, and you can even fit a full-size 10-by-14-inch Detroit pizza pan inside.

Preheating time is faster in a smaller oven, and that’s a selling point for the Arc Lite, with the stone reading around 750 degrees Fahrenheit at about 15 minutes. I’ve had the Arc Lite for several months, using it more than a handful of times for pizza night. The quick heat-up time is by far my favorite aspect of it. Instead of having to plan ahead and let the stone get to temp, I’m able to turn it on and just a few minutes later launch a pizza.

Granted, it does take more time between pizzas to get the stone back to temperature (the small stone doesn’t hold onto heat as well as the massive stones in bigger ovens), but during laid-back family pizza nights when the kids can’t make up their mind about what they want and I’m sneaking a slice instead of getting the next pizza ready, there’s enough time for the stone to get hot enough.

In some ways, that’s a selling point of the Arc Lite for those who are just starting out making pizza at home, where every aspect of just getting the pizza in the oven feels intimidating and overwhelming. The last thing you want to worry about at that point is burning the pizza.

At $399, the Arc Lite is easily the best budget-friendly pizza oven I’ve tried, and I’d even say it’s the best for pizza beginners too. It heats up fast, has a flame that rolls across the entire housing for even heating, and does exactly what you’d want a home pizza oven to do.

Fuel type: Gas | Cooking area: 1 12-inch pizza | Stone thickness: 12 mm | Temperature gauge:Analog | Dimensions: 19.1 x 16.5 x 12.6 inches | Weight: 29.7 pounds

Most home pizza ovens are big, heavy, and awkward to carry (if you can carry them at all). The Gozney Tread is the exact opposite of that. It’s purposely designed to be portable and used in all sorts of scenarios, like at the park for a picnic or at a campground in the middle of nowhere. Admittedly, carrying pizza dough and all of the toppings to remote locations isn’t something I’d want to do or even suggest, but Gozney has designed the Tread as more of a mobile kitchen than a single-purpose pizza oven.

The Tread isn’t the lightest oven I tested — that honor goes to Gozney’s Arc Lite at 26.4 pounds — but at just shy of 30 pounds, it’s not a struggle to move around, and Gozney has some accessories that reinforce its portability. The Venture Stand looks and works like a photography tripod (and collapses similarly for compact storage and travel), with the Tread slotting directly onto the top with a quick-release mechanism. There’s also a Roof Rack — a prep station that sits atop the oven, with a removable cutting board, giving you a spot to place and cut pizza or stow hot pans. Finally, the Venture Bag fits the Tread and Roof Rack, giving you an easy and tidy way to carry the entire setup.

You adjust the Tread’s temperature with a dial on the right side of the housing. On the same side there’s an analog temperature gauge with color-coded markings to let you know when the oven is at the right temp. The burner is on the left side of the Tread, and like bigger Gozney ovens, it is designed to push the flame up and roll it across the top of the chamber and down the right side, evenly heating the baking stone underneath it.

As for using it to actually make pizza — it’s a fun oven to use! It’s small but can easily handle 12-inch pizzas with no issues. There’s also more than enough space for a cast-iron skillet to make practically anything you want. Heat-up time was quick; the Tread’s baking stone reached 900 degrees Fahrenheit at exactly 20 minutes. I was able to push six pizzas through in under 25 minutes, with its 12-mm. stone providing respectable heat retention. It’s nearly the same experience as the Arc Lite, which uses the same size of stone. Neither of these ovens are designed to be high-volume machines, however — the point is to take your time and have fun.

If I had gone any faster, the stone would not have had time to come up to temperature between pizzas, but it’s more than good enough for someone who is hosting a small party or making pizza for family pizza night.

If I had to nitpick anything about the Tread, it’s that, as in the Arc Lite and other smaller ovens, I found it difficult to use a turning peel to rotate a pizza during the bake — there just isn’t quite enough room to work. Instead, I had to use a standard pizza peel to remove the pie, turn it, then place it back into the oven — but that’s expected with a smaller oven. Or maybe I’m just not skilled enough to maneuver a pizza on a turning peel in confined spaces.

The Tread’s quick setup — no matter where you are — combined with its small footprint, reliable performance, and suite of accessories make it a very attractive pizza oven for those who want to take their passion for pizza on the road or camping or to a family reunion.

Fuel type: Electric | Cooking area: 1 12-inch pizza | Stone thickness: 10 mm | Temperature gauge: Digital with presets | Dimensions: 21.5 x 17.4 x 10.4 inches | Weight: 38.8 pounds

Electric ovens have a distinct advantage over gas or wood-fueled ovens: You can use them indoors. So when I was recently asked if I could cater a small office party for about ten people, I instantly said “yes” and figured it would be the perfect opportunity to put the Volt 2 to the test. For the job, I used both the original Volt and the Volt 2 to get through 12 pizzas (six in each) in just under 30 minutes.

The overall design changes between the two — the Volt 2 has a larger viewing window, even with a smaller overall footprint — were apparent and welcome. The Volt 2 is small enough to fit on a standard countertop with room to spare.

The Volt 2 heats up to its max temperature of 850 degrees Fahrenheit in about 20 minutes. Setting and adjusting the temperature is done using a single dial on the front, along with buttons for preset bake settings based on pizza style; you can also save two custom presets so you don’t have to fine-tune your settings every time you turn it on, ensuring you don’t forget what temps work for your dough. There’s even a dough-proofing mode you can use to speed up your dough at temps as low as 70 degrees. Naturally, there’s a timer feature as well.

There’s enough space inside the oven to make a 12-inch pizza directly on the stone. Or if you’d rather make a Detroit-style pizza, the 13.3-inch square cook surface is big enough for an 8-by-10 pan (or Ooni’s 13-by-10 Detroit pan). Included with the Volt 2 is an oven rack you can place atop the stone; you can then place a baking sheet full of cookies or, really, anything else you want on the rack.

I was nervous about heat retention with the Volt 2’s 10-mm.-thick stone, but the Volt 2 had no problem keeping up with a pizza every few minutes. I found that if I triggered Boost mode (which temporarily diverts power to the top heating element, in turn supercharging the baking stone underneath) as I removed a pizza, the stone was ready for the next pizza by the time I had shaped and topped it.

The Volt 2’s versatility, quick heat-up time, ease of use, compact design, and $700 price tag make it the electric pizza oven to beat.

Fuel type: Gas, wood | Cooking area: 1 18-inch pizza, 2 12-inch pizzas, or 3 10-inch pizzas| Stone thickness: 30 mm | Temperature gauge: Digital with both stone and air temperature, along with food probe support | Dimensions: 27.4 x 37.2 x 39.2 inches | Weight: 161 pounds

The Gozney Dome XL (Gen 2) is a beast. For starters, it ships on a pallet, which arrives via a semitruck, and it’s packed in a box that’s full of reminders that you’ll need four people to lift it. It weighs 161 pounds, measures over three feet wide by nearly 28 inches deep, and with the ventilation pipe, is almost 40 inches tall. It’s big. Oh, and it has a baking stone that’s 1.18 inches thick.

In addition to its overall size, it’s expensive. The model I tested starts at $2,800 for just the oven. A stand will run you another $500, though it is a fantastic, useful addition that makes working with and moving the oven around a breeze. You can get a cover to keep off rain and snow between uses; an oven door for baking, smoking, and slow cooking; and even a Neapolitan arch for high-heat pizza cooking. (There is a smaller and lower-priced Dome (Gen 2), with enough space for two 10-inch pizzas that starts at $2,300, if you’re not sold on quite such a large oven.)

The second-generation Dome XL is a multi-fuel oven, allowing you to use gas, wood, or charcoal based on your personal preference. I did my testing with propane gas. For those who want to use wood, for another $200, Gozney’s Wood-Fire Control Kit adds improved airflow and a rack to keep ash and coals in place.

The oven’s internal dimensions — 28.5 inches wide by 21.4 inches deep by 9.4 inches high — translate into enough cooking space for three 10-inch pizzas, which I was able to confirm with plenty of room to spare. Actually, I think with some care I could get four 10-inch pizzas inside the oven. It would be tight, but it’s certainly possible.

A single burner on the left side of the XL, which emits a flame big enough to arc up and over the entire cooking surface, evenly heats the stone below it. You can monitor the ambient air and stone temperature using the digital console (this is the only oven I’ve ever used that displays both temperatures), thanks to its dual temperature setup — one sensor under the stone, another inside the cook area The gauge also has a built-in timer and supports plugging temperature probes into it so you can monitor the cooking temp of meat.

The first time I used the Dome XL, I followed the same preheat protocol as I did with the rest of the ovens. I took my first temp reading at 20 minutes, at which time the ambient temp read 863 degrees, while the bottom of the stone registered 574 degrees. That’s too low to get the classic char of Neapolitan pizza, so I let it warm up for another five minutes, when the temps read 904 and 655 degrees, respectively.

That said, because the baking stone is so thick, it takes time for the heat to saturate it and get the entire thing to temp. Gozney recommends preheating for 40- to 45 minutes, which is how long it took for me to start to see a consistent bottom bake. I launched the first test pizza at 30 minutes, and the bottom lacked any dark spots. However, by the 50-minute mark, when I had three pizzas inside at the same time, the bottoms came out perfect.

The Dome XL is by far the most capable oven I’ve used outside of the 48-inch wood-fired oven on my pizza trailer. It takes a little longer to heat up to a reliable temp than some of its smaller competitors, but it’s going to power through as many pizzas as you can push through it in a given night.

If you’re looking for the best home pizza oven money can buy, this is it.

The Karu 2 uses Ooni’s iconic glass-door design from its early pizza ovens. It’s sold as a wood-fired oven first, with an optional $120 gas-burner attachment. It’s a nice oven, but I found the gas burner to be finicky and difficult to light. After multiple attempts, following Ooni’s directions to the letter, with no luck, I resorted to using a lighter.

I’ve had the Koda 2 Max since it launched and have easily made over 100 pizzas in it during that time. It heats up fast, has solid heat retention, and is big enough to bake three pizzas at once — though it’s really cramped compared to the Gozney Dome XL (Gen 2).

If you want an oven that’s big enough to crank out pizzas for a party and don’t want to splurge on the Dome XL, the $1,299 Koda 2 Max is worth considering.

Like the Ooni Koda 2 Max, I’ve had the Arc XL since it launched and have used it to make countless pizzas. The total has to be in the hundreds. It has been my go-to and the oven I’ve recommended to friends and family without question. However, at $999, it’s hard to recommend it over Ooni’s Koda 2 Pro as the best overall pizza oven. They’re similar in size, but the Koda 2 Pro has more room inside for multiple pizzas and some extra nice-to-have features, tipping the scales ever so slightly in its favor. Not everyone agrees, however — and Strategist senior writer Michael Zhao (who’s also tested both models extensively) prefers the Arc XL.

If you prefer Gozney’s overall aesthetic and accessory package (they truly do make the best pizza stands out there), and if you can get it on sale when the prices are more equivalent, then the Arc XL will surely make you a happy pizza-maker.

I really liked this small oven. It’s portable, easy to move between counter and patio or to put away in the pantry for storage. It got to temp fast and did a good job with reheating between pizzas. I’d have no complaints about using it on a regular basis. But it’s expensive at $1,000, and a limited cooking surface with a backstop prevents you from putting anything larger in the oven. The Ooni Volt 2 is more versatile and simply a better value.

entry.title: Everything You Need to Make the Perfect Dirty Martini at Home
entry.summary: The ideal tools, plus olives that come with extra brine.
entry.content:
The dirty martini has been through a lot. As I discovered while writing my cookbook, The Little Book of Olives, the drink has been taken to salty extremes with smoked salmon, pickles, giardiniera, MSG — even potlikker. It’s been turned to slush, made fizzy, and (somehow) grilled. In fits of studious research, I’ve consumed $30 martinis in hotel lounges with Sinatra look-alikes playing live piano music and $15 martinis in dive bars accompanied with crinkly bags of potato chips.

After all this, my favorite dirty martini is still the one made at home, with London dry gin, a no-frills white vermouth (I like Dolin), and really good green olives that are packed in pure brine. A martini at home will be much colder than one that took a labyrinthine ten-minute journey through a steakhouse to get to your table. Even better, it’s an opportunity to perfectly customize the drink to your dream proportions, whether you prefer a drink that’s restrained in its salinity or one that borders on soup. Here are a few of the tools and ingredients that you should be using to make this classic cocktail perfectly.

Don’t believe the James Bond propaganda — shaking your gin, vermouth, and olive brine together will leave it cloudy, full of ice shards, and way too diluted. For a clear, cold, velvety-textured martini, stir it in a glass full of ice. Technically, any glass can be a cocktail-mixing glass if it’s roomy enough to fit a few handfuls of ice and about three ounces of liquor, but the classic design for this piece of barware works so well that it’s hard to resist. There’s a heavy bottom that keeps the glass stable while you rapidly stir its contents and a diamond-cut pattern that makes it easier to firmly grip, and the spout helps you pour with precision, even into your daintiest glasses. Mine doubles as a flower vase when it’s off-duty.

How do you keep all that ice from cannonballing into your glass (not to mention the olive fragments that may have cruised in with the splash of brine you added)? With a Hawthorne strainer, which fits snugly over the top of your cocktail-mixing glass so that you can strain and pour at the same time with only one hand.

To stir a Manhattan or martini rapidly for the 15 to 30 seconds it takes to fully chill, it helps to have a spoon that gently cups the ice in the glass while swiveling easily in your hand. Enter the barspoon, which you’ll also find yourself reaching for to stir honey into iced tea and milk into cold brew.

These pitted Gordal olives are packed with extra brine so you won’t run out if you’re making dirty martinis for a roomful of people. Because this varietal is so much larger than your average Manzanilla or Castelvetrano, these are also a sturdy option if you want to stuff your olives with blue cheese (or … crab-rangoon filling).

When I’m not stuffing olives for martinis, I prefer the firm texture and fruity taste of a green olive with its pit intact. These bright-green Castelvetranos from Partanna add a mild, sophisticated saltiness to martinis, and you’ll want to snack on every one that doesn’t make it into your drink.

If you’ve sipped a glass of iced vermouth in Spain, you’ve probably encountered Manzanillas, which are one of the most ubiquitous types of green olives in the country. These from Bernal have a complex, almost smoky flavor that comes from a brining technique that’s been refined over the company’s 125-year history.

Nothing makes you feel like you’re drinking a martini in a fancy steakhouse like a weighty stainless-steel cocktail pick. No splinters of bamboo lodged in your olives and no unnecessary waste — just an elegant bar accessory that clinks satisfyingly against the glass every time you take a sip.

entry.title: The Best Gift Is a Vintage Kids’ Book
entry.summary: Rediscover a childhood favorite.
entry.content:
Of course, you can’t go wrong with Goodnight, Moon. But one of the greatest gifts the internet has given parents is that many of the out-of-print books of their youth are available to buy online — and if you’re lucky, with the 1987 library binding still intact. And even if they’re not necessarily out of print, rediscovering vintage titles is a delight — and also make an unexpected present. I asked 37 authors, illustrators, writers, booksellers, artists, and other bookish people to share their childhood favorites. Below are 76 vintage or otherwise hard-to-find treasures that make excellent gifts for every age. If you prefer to buy a new edition, many of the forgotten classics have been reissued for the modern reader. For even more children’s book ideas, here’s a roundup of 2026 releases.

“I love the entire cute, bizarre oeuvre of Harry Whittier Frees. He illustrated a bunch of cats, but the illustrations are actually photographs (really). There’s Four Little Kittens and Whiskers, which is the best one, IMO, but impossible to find. Toodles and Her Friends, which features a rabbit and a dog, is great, too. He did not limit it to just cats!”

“This Richard Scarry set rules, and I don’t know why it’s not been reissued. It’s all real vehicles, as opposed to the fanciful oddities in his Busytown books. Both of my kids looked at this for hours and hours as small children. The books are kind of strangely shaped, these tall rectangles, in this way that is very pleasing. I think it’s a great baby shower gift, and I have given it more than once.”

“It’s hard to pick just one Remy Charlip book but Fortunately is a great place to start. It is about a series of events that alternately go very well or very badly while a poor kid just tries to get to a party. Charlip was an incredible illustrator, designer, and all around creative guy and this book is one of his best.”

“The Big Jump is a collection of three stories about a weird kingdom and some people who live there and have to deal with weird rules, riddles, and bad kings. It’s loose and funny and strange and it was my favorite when I was little.”

“Again, tough to pick a Steig. This has some of the most frightening moments of any picture book I’ve ever read, not for their fantastic or magic qualities, but for how weirdly real they seem. A young girl pig finds a talking bone in the woods right before a fox kidnaps her and brings her home to his house to eat. Steig never missed, and this is one of his most memorable books, I think.”

“I am embarrassed by how much I spent to get this out-of-print book by Leo Hartas from my childhood for my daughter, but it’s truly the most comforting, magical, engaging cross section of an old-fashioned apartment building. It teaches kids about everything from architectural details to plumbing to neighborly relations. An illustrated dollhouse with lessons!”

“The Marcel Marceau Counting Book was given to our daughter by the artist Lee Mary Manning, whose own work has something of the same playfulness and sensitivity to gesture. The great French mime Marcel Marceau counts from one to 20 by putting on a succession of hats. He is alternately a cowboy, a farmer, a swordsman, a jockey, and eventually his beloved character Bip. With every new hat, another character appears, and the discarded hats gradually accumulate into a kind of sculpture. I love that children learn to count almost incidentally, while watching someone become 20 different people simply by changing his hat.”

“Published as part of the beautiful little King Penguin series, A Book of Toys traces the history of toys through Gwen White’s illustrations, based on objects in British museum collections. There are ancient rattles, little bronze animals, a Roman wooden horse whose wheels have fallen off, and toys made of clay, string, paper, and tin. I love the idea that children have been playing with versions of the same things for thousands of years. Each object is given a personality, and the book feels like a miniature museum of childhood.”

“Bruno Munari was one of the great Italian artists and designers of the 20th century. I was introduced to his work by the gallery Kaufmann Repetto. Created as part of a series inspired by his young son Alberto, this book follows an eccentric animal seller offering increasingly improbable pets: a pipe-smoking flamingo, a slightly tipsy armadillo, a grumpy porcupine, even a centipede to take for a walk. The pages are cut to different sizes, with flaps and windows that reveal unexpected details as you turn them. The book itself becomes a kind of toy. It’s funny, surreal, and beautifully designed.”

“I am obsessed with mazes and have been since my dad drew them on napkins to entertain me as a child during dinners out. I continue this practice today with my son. He and I love this book of mazes, which you solve by tracing your finger through the pages. O’er hill and dale and lava and bridge and castle steps and rope ladder and secret trapdoor you will go. Each segment is so detailed and wondrous, I sometimes don’t want to find the end.”

“Suzuki Beane is the beatnik Eloise. She lives with artists Hugh and Marcia in a pad on Bleecker Street. They are also, I might add, her parents. I got my copy 15 years ago at Powell’s Books in Portland, and the price has certainly gone up. The drawings are by Louise Fitzhugh, who wrote and illustrated Harriet the Spy, another essential NYC gal-about-town. My friend Anya is kind of the real-life Suzuki. This book is a treasure that makes me want to hit the pavement.”

“A classic. Everyone should read it.”

“Punk. Perfect. I read it around when it was published, when I was about four. The reason I️ want to make kids’ books.”

“Just really, really funny. I️ think it’s all in the pictures but I’m biased.”

“I Am a Bunny is obvious, but I cannot read that book without getting teary-eyed because it’s about this hopeful/hopeless optimism before adulthood falls. I think it’s about depression, or at least melancholy: ‘I live in a hollow log.’ First editions aren’t going for big dollars, but they look beautiful. The illustrations are wonderful.”

“Poppy and Mozart and Poppy and Vivaldi are interactive books that play songs when you press on buttons. They’re charming, whimsical, and my son couldn’t get enough. They’re new-ish but fell out of print in the United States. They’re just not around.”

“When they were younger, my boys especially liked Dorothy Kunhardt’s Junket is Nice and Now Open the Box. They used to spend hours with Claude Ponti’s older books Blaze and the Castle Cake for Bertha Daye and Le doudou méchant, which I don’t believe has been translated into English, as well as Graeme Base’s The Eleventh Hour which remains a favorite. We try to pick up some hardback Nancy Drews and Hardy Boys books whenever we’re in a used bookshop. They love comics — Nancy and Sluggo’s Guide to Life, all of Peanuts and Calvin and Hobbes, Mafalda, etc. — and all the MinaLima books, although I don’t know if you can get them in the U.S.”

“As older readers, they’ve enjoyed this lushly illustrated edition of E. Nesbit’s The Enchanted Castle and Edward Eager’s Half Magic (although some of the dialogue at the end is racially insensitive). My older son’s class just finished reading The Westing Game, which was hugely enjoyable for him. In August, he read Lord of the Flies, which he liked much more than the treacly books his school assigns as summer reading. Last year, after we watched Lupin on Netflix, he read the Macmillan Collectors’ edition of Arsène Lupin, Gentleman Thief. My younger son has recently finished A Cricket in Times Square, which is wry and wonderful, and we read Maniac Magee together last spring.”

“Frank and Ernest, by Alexandra Day. Frank and Ernest are a manlike bear and a slightly less manlike —but still pretty manlike — elephant, who wear beautifully tailored suits and do temp work. They get jobs running a diner (for humans). But the most absurd thing in this book is the English language. Frank and Ernest revel in the strange argot of a restaurant kitchen — ‘Paint a bow-wow red, Frank, and I need a nervous pudding.’ It’s hilarious, and it has a very weird, very poignant last page.”

“Shortcut, by Donald Crews. What a thrill it is to read this story aloud, and to have it read to you! Donald Crews has one of the greatest bodies of work in all of children’s literature. Freight Train is his most famous book; Shortcut is my favorite. It brings together Crews’s genius for storytelling and book design to follow some kids who have a harrowing adventure on the railroad tracks. There’s not another picture book like it, not even close.”

“Caleb & Kate, William Steig. Again and again, William Steig wrote about characters who undergo a magical transformation, but each story wrings something new from the premise. Caleb & Kate is about an argument—the heat, the remorse, the isolation, the reconciliation. I grew up in a house where we argued a lot, and this book is dead-on, even though neither my mom nor I was ever transformed into a dog by a capricious witch.”

“The Sun Egg, by Elsa Beskow. It’s definitely still in print, but it’s an old book and has a few wacky turns of phrase that I think add to its appeal. My kids (5 and almost 3) love it and have for quite some time! It’s about a little elf who loves to dance and who one day comes across what she thinks is an egg that the sun has laid.”

“This wonderful, funny book was the first in a series from the ‘80s by Barbara Samuels that is sadly, now largely out of print. Duncan and Dolores is about a rascally young girl named Dolores who has a somewhat bumpy journey to learning how to meet her new cat Duncan where he is (under the bed) and not where she wants him to be (in a brass band with her). Since I have always been a criminal over-snuggler of pets, this book appealed to me on a psychic level — plus, my mom’s work as a performer of this book at bedtime was particularly good (we still quote one of her “line readings” to each other). Now, 35 years later, I still love reading this book to my kids — it’s still my favorite kind of kids book: funny and deep without clobbering anyone over the head with a Very Important Life Lesson.”

“My friend Fanny gave me Gennarino ‘for my kids,’ but it was really a present for me: the story of a young Italian boy who wishes for a bigger fishing boat with gorgeous 1960s illustrations? Couldn’t possibly be more up my alley. Luckily my daughters humor me on occasion and let me include it in our bedtime short stack, and we pretend that it appeals to us all equally.”

“Ruth Chew books were some of my favorite books as a child; I’m always surprised that they aren’t better-known. They usually consist of an everyday child (many times in Brooklyn, I remember really wanting to see Prospect Park) finding or receiving a magical item and their subsequent adventures. They were all charming and delightful and to 7-year-old me, very exciting! This one features magic buttons, which has made me always look at any button with appreciation.”

“Natalie Babbit is known for her book Tuck Everlasting but my favorite of hers is The Search for Delicious. I particularly love the first edition where she illustrated the cover as well as the interiors. This book was one of my inspirations for Where the Mountain Meets the Moon; it made me want to write about a journey that was like a fairytale.”

“Carolyn Haywood books were also influential books of my childhood — they inspired my Year of the Dog books. I loved how they showed so much of my everyday life — school, friends, neighborhood, and this one in particular always feels like Christmas to me. Betsy’s Little Star features Betsy’s younger sister who was born on Christmas and is so named Star.”

“The Tall Book of Make Believe illustrated by Garth William is an anthology of stories and poems edited by Jane Werner. Its unusual tall and thin format made it standout from all my other books on my childhood shelf. I poured over my copy - over and over again - completely captivated by the many color and black and white illustrations by Garth Williams. It remains one of my all time favorite picture book treasures!”

“As a young boy, I was mesmerized by the art in this lovely picture book by Charlotte Zolotow and illustrated by Maurice Sendak. It had an ethereal and gentle quality that set it apart from most of the picture books at the time.”

“I remember being at my hometown library when I was in second grade and I was exploring the children’s room. The cover of Millions of Cats caught my eye. The book was so different than the typical picture book; it was dark and bold. The text was hand-lettered which was also quite different than most picture books. This probably influenced me to use my own handwriting for almost all my own picture books. The story was originally published in 1928 and won a Newbery Honor award in 1929. Millions of Cats is the oldest American picture book still in print.”

“One of my favorite books as a child was The Happy Lion. It was one of the few books that I saved and read with my own children, who loved it as much as I did. The story is about a beloved lion at a zoo in France who is visited by the townspeople each day who call out, ‘Bonjour, Happy Lion.’ One day, when his cage is left unlocked, he wanders out into the streets, intending to visit his friends, who, much to his surprise, greet him with shrieks of dismay. A lion in a cage is one thing, a lion loose on the streets is another. Only a small boy is sensible enough to know that the happy lion is the same happy lion, caged or loose, and together the two walk with dignified calm back to the zoo. There’s a whole lot to love about this genial lion and wise child, not least of all Duvoisin’s beautiful and endearing drawings. My 3-year-old child was obsessed with this book and greeted everyone with ‘Bonjour’ for quite some time. It was out of print but reissued on its 50th anniversary in 2004.”

“The Agony in the Kindergarten is not really a book for children so much as it is a book about children, and the adults who misunderstand them. Hilarious and agonizing in equal measure, Steig pairs wildly inventive line drawings with acutely observant text — the things grown-ups say about their children when they don’t think they can hear. It is a work of genius, I’m sure it made me a better parent, and I buy copies whenever I see them pop up on eBay or in a secondhand bookstore.”

“I grew up on this lavishly illustrated unabridged version of Collodi’s Pinocchio. The book is surreal, haunting and as unsettling as entering someone else’s dreams. I loved it as a kid and when I look through it now, I can see how deeply it impacted my imagination.”

“Mary Norton’s The Borrowers is over 60 years old now, but the magic of tiny people who live in the floorboards of our houses never grows old. I was enchanted with these books (there are five in the series) when I was a kid. They still enchant me as an adult.”

“The Watsons Go to Birmingham – 1963 by Christopher Paul Curtis is (unbelievably) more than 30 years old. This funny, warm, wise book is one of the reasons I am a writer of books for children. It is a master class in looking at difficult things through a child’s eyes.”

“These were the first figurative paintings I was ever really into. I remember winning the book is a raffle at my local bookstore the week that it came out. I wasn’t much of a reader then, but the style and ambition of this was mesmerising. Written in the style of a long forgotten journal, it is an incredible achievement.”

“The power of mindset and perspective are the main tools at play here. Written in the old-timey style of the pioneering West, this is a book I discovered back in art school, around the time I was beginning to think about making a book of my own. It opened my eyes to the sheer variety of picture books out there, and to just how powerfully they could work at portraying real life morals seamlessly into very entertaining narratives.”

“This is a book I remember from the early ‘80s, and I cite often as an influence. Less well known than Carle’s The Very Hungry Caterpillar, this grouchy ladybug (or bad tempered ladybird to use the British English translation), is in a bad mood and tries to pick fights with increasingly larger animals until she gets all the way up to a whale. The book seemed like a magic trick as the whale seemed so enormous in its gatefold spread, and it was with this spread at the tender age of, maybe 5, that I discovered the power of scale in art.”

“Carol Kendall’s The Gammage Cup is a gentle fantasy from 1959 so utterly charming it didn’t need to sprawl into a series. The Minnipins live in the Land Between the Mountains, on the banks of the Watercress River, and their folkways and eccentricities are given space to flower as the peaceful status quo is about to change. Like Dune, each chapter begins with a fictional epigraph — a scrap of poetry or philosophy, including one by an appealingly absent-minded Minnipin named Muggles. The Gammage Cup is worth all of Harry Potter put together.”

“I love that Scholastic put out an H.P. Lovecraft anthology. The Shadow Over Innsmouth and Other Stories of Horror (1971) is a perfect primer to the author’s brand of cosmic fright, complete with spectral cover art and introductions by Margaret Ronan. (’What kind of Christmas story would you expect H.P. Lovecraft to write?’ she asks before ‘The Festival,’ a story featuring The Necronomicon. ‘Uncozy? Unmerry? Certainly uncanny.’) ‘The Colour Out of Space’ and the title story bookend shorter fictions, including ‘The Outsider’ and a tale Lovecraft ghostwrote for Houdini.”

“Song of the Swallows, by Leo Politi. This picture book about the return of the swallows to San Juan Capistrano might have been the first book I ever read featuring a Latino character. I still remember it.”

“The Talking Eggs is one of my favorite picture books. A magical Creole folktale about kindness.”

“Bullfrog Grows Up, by Rosamond Dauer, illustrated by Byron Barton. A short and sweet story about a mouse family who find and raise a tadpole into adulthood. Sometimes you have to embark on your own once you’ve outgrown something, in this case literally!”

“Milk and Cookies, by Frank Asch. This book made me decide chocolate chip cookies were the best. Also a great story about imagination and fear alongside very satisfying illustrations.”

“Joan Steiner constructed colorful scenes out of everyday objects deployed in surprising and clever ways in her Look-Alikes series. Look closely at the ‘microwave’ in a kitchen scene and you’ll find that it’s actually a wallet and two dominoes — and the dish rack is a hair clip! An outer-space scene features a ‘rocket’ made from a Thermos, a shuttlecock, a piece of rotini pasta and some erasers. The process of decoding is delightful and the scenes are lovingly tactile. Plus it’s a fun way to teach your kid words like thimble or protractor or dentures or harmonica.”

“I just bought this for my kids. Crucially, it has to be spiral-bound, with the measuring spoons, and with the bears on the cover. This book taught me how to cook as a kid, and I hope it will do the same for my increasingly cooking-curious kids (8 and 11) who I still don’t totally trust with a sharp knife, though Raffi has been making himself ramen a lot recently. The recipes are a) GOOD and b) both easy enough and challenging enough to motivate kids to be more independent in the kitchen. I’m hoping to outsource making dinner eventually.”

“We love the Meg and Mog books by Helen Nicoll and Jan Pienkowksi. This series is from my own childhood; we actually have a copy that belonged to me. My older son loves witches and stories where things don’t go as planned. Personally, I find the illustrations so pleasing and bold.

“We also like Almond Cookies and Dragon Well Tea by Cynthia Chin-Lee. I only recently discovered it, maybe in the last year or so. We love books about families, generational homes, and traditions that get passed down.”

“Take Time to Relax: If there were an N+1 Bookmatch just for kids, this would be my top rec. A family of Beavers are burnt out on their schedule of extremely ‘90s extracurriculars (karate, aerobics, computer class) when they unexpectedly get snowed in. Now they have no choice but to chill! A precious relic from the pre-Zoom era, when a day off really was a day off.”

“Tomi Ungerer was a superb storyteller, and he never sentimentalized children. His stories are delightfully bizarre and captivating. Phaidon has reissued several beautiful editions of his work, but this one is still out of print for now.”

“I love this lesser-known story by Margaret Wise Brown. A group of children find a dead bird in the woods. They wrap it in leaves, bury it, and sing to it every day, until they forget. The story was reissued in 2016 with new illustrations, but the original, with Remy Charlip’s muted blues and greens, is the one to find. Like the writers I admire most, Brown doesn’t explain or console; she just lets children do what children do.”

“Mr. Postmouse Takes a Trip, about a mouse mail carrier traveling the world with his family, has a Wes Anderson–meets–Richard Scarry sort of appeal. There are little easter eggs on every page that keep rereads interesting. I appreciate the message behind the mouse family making friends everywhere they go, from mountaintop marmots to a dragon living inside a volcano.”

“This book is part of a set in which the author reports almost prosaic events from the voice of a preschool-age narrator, each managing, with the sparest of text, to reveal something profound about the experience of being a child.”

“Maurice Sendak spoke about the relationship between picture books and music, and this one really exemplifies how a book can be a song and dance unto itself, from two of the best to ever do it.”

“Kids prank the teachers, teachers prank the kids, and the reader wins in this quintessential picture book set at school.”

“What I respect most about old children’s books is that they aren’t pandering to the adults in the room who feel like every story should teach a lesson. The narratives are discursive, they are abstract, they are weird, they are dissonant … as in, they are actually written for children’s minds. (If the Rands sound familiar to you, Paul, Ann’s spouse, was a graphic designer in the mid-century.)”

“This book is the ultimate nostalgia: It’s a book for kids from the perspective of grown-up kids remembering their own childhoods playing in an imaginary village they built out of rocks, in the desert. It’s funny and sweet — and totally meta for a parent remembering their own adolescence while reading to their child!”

“Every night when I was growing up, my dad would read a couple of chapters of some long book to us (ahem, The Hobbit). He introduced my two daughters to this series about two toad brothers, Warton and Morton, and reads it to them in daily installments whenever he comes to stay with us from across the country.”

“A House is a House for Me is rhyming, which always brings the kids along, but the whole concept is thinking of increasingly abstract things that can be houses for other things — like a jar is a house for a pickle, things like that. It’s a kind of jolly weirdness that I think kids books really used to have a lot more.”

“On Market Street is an ABC book but has the most amazing outlandish illustrations— every letter is represented by a person made up of things that start with that letter. A ribbon lady for the letter R, a zipper man for Z. I also read it as a kid and those images stayed with me. And I love that idea of having a shared visual history with my kids. It makes me feel like we are connecting on some epigenetic level of imagination!”

“50 Watts Books specializes in reissues of international picture books. Some of my favorites: Animal Land Where There Are No People, A Tiger in the Land of Dreams, I Am A Wolf, After All, and The King of Circles.”

“And some of my all-time favorite picture books to give as gifts: Arm in Arm by Remy Charlip; The Rainbow Goblins by Ulde Rico; Zoom by Istvan Banyai (you could do a whole series of wordless picture books: Journey, Il Pallocino Rosso…); Piggybook — very off first wave feminist text with great illustrations; and Could be Worse! — a good gift for a grandparent. This is out of print: When I’m Big by Dick Bruna (creator of Miffy)”

“This was my favorite book as a kid. I got it when I was maybe 4 years old — I might have been younger — but when I became sentient it was there. I loved it so much because it was my birthday and the book was about his birthday. The one I had, there were flaps so you could discover things behind the presents, which I enjoyed.”

“One of the authors whose books should only be bought in their vintage condition is Ellen Raskin. Raskin was a polymath who moved from art form to art form: first graphic design, then book illustration and design, writing and illustrating picture books, and ultimately writing (and illustrating!) children’s fiction. She lavished care on all the parts of a reader’s experience, designing the cover art and illustrating the novels herself.

Raskin came back to certain themes again and again: Loneliness and the value of kindred spirits. Art, craft, and commerce. Hope after pain. (The author knew of what she spoke; she suffered from a painful disease that ended her life far too soon.) And … puzzles, puzzles, puzzles. A complete set of early editions of her novels would make a terrific gift for the type of middle schooler who likes escape rooms: The Westing Game, Figgs & Phantoms, The Mysterious Disappearance of Leon (I Mean Noel), and The Tattooed Potato and Other Clues. Younger children will enjoy her visually inventive picture books like Spectacles and Franklin Stein.”

“Before it was transformed into Tchaikovsky’s ballet, The Nutcracker was a children’s tale by German Romantic author E. T. A. Hoffmann. The story is stranger and darker than the version audiences have come to know — fittingly for Hoffmann, whose gothic works inspired the likes of Edgar Allan Poe and featured in Freud’s The Uncanny. Maurice Sendak disliked the sugar-coating of life for children, so when he had the opportunity to do set and costume design for a staging of The Nutcracker, he embraced the story’s macabre elements. After the ballet, Sendak released his own surreal illustrated edition of Hoffmann’s story. The book is still in print, but a vintage copy signed by the late Sendak would make a truly special gift for a young dancer with a spooky streak.”

“Margaret Mahy was New Zealand’s Roald Dahl, but with greater warmth. She remains a giant in her native land, but is less known here. Her Tick Tock Tales is a collection of witty, inventive tales with offbeat twists. Mahy shines in the deadpan moments so rarely allowed into today’s picture books — as when a sailor tells a magical sea-woman of his plan to rescue twenty orphans, and she responds ‘Indeed … I’ve often thought I’d like twenty boys myself.’ Reader, she marries him. Excellent for parents longing to elevate their bedtime read-alouds.”

“For me it’s always Gila Monsters Meet You at the Airport for every new parent. It’s exceptionally written, plausibly useful (is someone moving towns with a child?), and beautifully illustrated! I literally found my copy at my town’s dump. They have a giveaway section. And I’ve since always ordered all of the authors’ books for anyone pregnant, etc. She understands ‘writing for the parent.’”

“Lois Ehlert took photos of her folk art collection and used them as collage to make a story about going to the farmers market. Since our gallery is in Union Square, our daughter is very acquainted with farmers markets, so she loved it. (Nuts to You by the same author is a favorite).”

“Our daughter likes to look at books while she’s eating, so we go through a lot of material, and this 175-pager is sitting next to me as I write this. Arnold Lobel is best known for Frog and Toad, but he was very prolific, and they are all bangers. He’s a really good illustrator, and it’s pretty fun when your kid starts to recite all these nursery rhymes everywhere they go …”

“The Night Before Christmas, written by Clement C. Moore and illustrated by Gyo Fujikawa, is the most perfect Christmas book to give as a gift. From the first ornately detailed cutaway of the house to the final spread of Santa and his reindeer flying off into the sky, Gyo Fujikawa is delivering pure enchantment on every page. My favorite is the dreamy pile of sleeping children nestled under cakes, candies, and berry baskets on a bed of pink clouds.”

“This book introduces math concepts through art, illusions, and playful on-page games, rendered in gorgeous, precise watercolors and pen and ink by the Japanese artist and author Mitsumasa Anno. My 9-year-old begs to read this (and also Math Games II and III) over and over again, despite knowing all the answers. It’s a picture book but also an activity book and a play thing all in one.”

“This black-and-white picture book about a family journey from country to city and back again is sparse on words, but genius in concept. You read it front to back as you go to the city, then flip it over and read it back to front for the trip home. Jonas uses the power of negative space to create Rorschach-like images that tell a story in either orientation. It’s quiet and clever, with more to discover in the details on each read.”

“First published in 1969, this book is a true masterpiece: an amazing readaloud for a 4-to-8-ish-year-old kid, full of wordplay, with illustrations each miniature works of art. Charlip was a creative polymath, and his love of play comes alive on the page. This book is a collection of stories, poems, and word experiments. Some rhyme, others are recursive, and some are just befuddling. Charlip defies traditional left-to-write structures of storytelling, and words take on shapes that inform how you read them.”

“Enzo Mari’s The Fable Game consists of six large interlocking panels with illustrations of various farm animals and wildlife in both night and day scenarios. The illustrations are super simple and very charming, but the narrative possibilities are endless. I really love the simplicity of the illustrations. Originals can be tough to find and sometimes pricey, but reproductions can be found at Corraini Editions.”

entry.title: The Gadget Gifts Teens Want, According to Teens
entry.summary: Record players and Polaroids are out. CD players and digital cameras are in.
entry.content:
As someone who has covered teen gifts for the Strategist for the past couple of years, I’ve seen a lot of trends come and go. Within the tech space, things have shifted from record players and Polaroids to CD players and digital cameras. In that same vein, we’re seeing a resurgence of wired headphones and transparent tech. Some things, though, have remained constant: Apple still wins over any other brand of earbuds, and fun lighting is a must for room décor. To gather all the teen-approved gizmos and gadgets and gear in one place, I made this gift guide and sorted everything out by price point. There’s something for every teen — the gamer, the GRWM girl, the music lover, the athlete, and more. And, if you’re looking for more general gift ideas, I’ve written a gift guide for teen boys and a gift guide for teen girls, too.

If they don’t already have one, here’s an easy stocking stuffer for the teen filming fit-check and GRWM videos.

Everything from the ’90s and early aughts is cool again, including transparent tech and wired headphones.

Read more: The Kids Yearn for Transparent Tech

Another option that leans more toward the DIY aesthetic.

Most teens I spoke to are key chain maximalists with trinkets, tech, and beauty products in their collection. Go with something they’ll actually use day-to-day.

Not technically a gadget, but teens are obsessed with bedazzling everything — tech included. This comes with whatever they need to get started.

Lots of teens I spoke to want a fridge in their room to stock with sodas and skin care. This one even doubles as a cooler.

Scrolling through TikTok gave me a glimpse of what’s in teens rooms, and LED lights were in nearly every video. These are inexpensive and come with a handy remote for adjusting color and brightness.

If they’re into filming TikToks or vlogs, I rounded up a couple of inexpensive ways to upgrade their phone setup.

For the teen who’s constantly at 5 percent, gift them a power bank. This magnetic cordless option is fuss-free, and they’re less likely to lose it.

Read more: The 7 Best Portable Chargers

Here’s an all-in-one speaker and light from JBL. Our tech writer says it’s his new favorite Bluetooth speaker, since it features eye-catching moving lights, is louder than other travel-friendly options, and is super-compact.

If your teen is prone to misplacing their keys, backpack, or purse, they’ll appreciate the practicality of an AirTag. Pair with one of the fun covers above.

Since a lot of schools don’t allow phones in classrooms, teens are turning to good old-fashioned watches. Make sure it’s digital, durable, and distinct.

If they’re into gaming, go ahead and buy them a backup headset. Parents of gamers I spoke to said their teens go through at least two or three a year.

If they specifically like laptop gaming, consider this ’90s-inspired keyboard recommended by Joanna Nelius, a former laptop reviewer at the Verge and a lifelong gamer.

Multiple staffers are fans of the Camp Snap for its filmlike digital photos without the extra distraction of a screen. It’s also a cheaper option for younger teens who want to hop on the digital-camera trend.

Some teens have moved on from collecting records to collecting CDs. Instead of searching eBay, go with this model that has USB-C charging, anti-skip protection, and up to 48 hours of playback.

For a slightly fancier LED light setup, go with Philips’ strips. They have Bluetooth capabilities, so you can control colors and dimming from your phone.

iPad’s were top of teens’ wishlists last year. If they already have one, consider gearing them up with some accessories.

AirPods still reign supreme, especially for older teens.

Beats are close runners-up and a bit more popular with teens who play sports.

Digital cameras are still going strong this year over film and Polaroids.

They’re pricey, but a lot of teens mentioned this as their top gift. Reasons were across the board, from watching YouTube and gaming to journaling and making art.

A couple teens mentioned wanting a TV in their room. I suggest going with a projector like this. It’s easy to set up and portable, so older teens can bring it to college, too.

The wellness trend has trickled down to the teens. Most I spoke to prefer gold, but check your teen’s everyday jewelry before purchasing.

Every teen into content creation said this was their No. 1 wish-list item. It’s definitely pricey, but it’s worth noting that its popularity has continued to grow over the past few years.

Sony’s vlogging camera comes at a fraction of the price, and it’s just as compact and easy to use.

entry.title: Faux-Fur Blankets Are Everywhere. How Does the Cocoon Compare?
entry.summary: It’s like a lighter, slinkier version of the viral Lola blanket.
entry.content:
I’m the type of person who is nearly always wrapped in a throw blanket at home, and faux fur has always been my favorite style. The soft, plush feel and the weightiness of the material make for the ultimate cozy experience. Evidently, I’m far from the only person who feels that way: Faux-fur blankets are having a moment. Anthropologie has long made a popular one that comes in more than a dozen colors. Cozy Earth is constantly expanding its line of fuzzy fur throws. Lola Blankets are everywhere on social media feeds and in podcast ads. Brooklinen and furniture-maker Sixpenny even got in on the action this year.

Amid all of this faux-fur mania came the Cocoon blanket, which I first learned about when it launched in July. It seemed to be a direct competitor to the influencer- and celebrity-loved Lola, with slightly more elevated branding. The two brands’ prices are similar — $255 for a 60-inch-by-50-inch Cocoon blanket versus $275 for a 60-inch-by-50-inch Lola blanket — and the fabric composition is exactly the same: 95 percent polyester and 5 percent spandex. So I was naturally curious about how the Cocoon would compare.

I received my Cocoon blanket in August, and it rapidly become the favored throw blanket in my home. It’s the one I wrap myself in when I’m lounging on the couch to watch TV or read, and I’ve even slept with it on chilly nights. Friends gravitate toward it when they visit my apartment, and multiple people have asked me where I got it. I regularly find my two cats napping or making biscuits on the blanket; they are excellent judges of coziness, and I can reliably lure them to come sit with me when I have the Cocoon on my lap.

The Cocoon even dethroned another faux-fur blanket I quite like, the Bubble Cuddle blanket from Cozy Earth, because it’s a bit more comfortable to swaddle myself in. I think the difference comes down to the fabric composition — my Cozy Earth blanket is 100 percent polyester, while the Cocoon’s 5 percent spandex gives it a bit of stretch and makes it extra snuggly. The Cocoon is also double-layered, and while it’s not officially a weighted blanket (though Cocoon recently started selling those, too), it does have some heft. The material feels opulently soft and silky, with stitching that gives it a textured, rippled look, and it comes in multiple solid colors, striped patterns, and animal prints.

Two of my Strategist colleagues and fellow plush-blanket fans, Bella Druckman and Brenley Goertzen, have also tried the Cocoon and agree it’s among the softest blankets they’ve ever touched. Goertzen says it’s softer than her Little Moo, UnHide, and CB2 faux-fur blankets, and it has held up well to her dogs chewing bones on it, nesting in it, and digging in it. Druckman, who tested the Lola blanket earlier this year, called the Cocoon a strong competitor to the Lola that ultimately just feels a little different: “I often describe the Lola as soft, like what I would imagine petting a chinchilla would feel like. It’s faux, but it has somewhat of a real fur quality to it,” she says. “The Cocoon is much silkier and slinkier in comparison.” Though she likes the respective feel of each blanket, she prefers the Lola overall, as she says it keeps her warmer and feels like more of a true heavyweight blanket. So which one is right for you will likely come down to personal preference.

Both the Lola and the Cocoon are machine washable, but neither can be dried with heat, and since laundering faux fur can be tricky, I was nervous about how my Cocoon would fare. After washing it on cold, I ran it through my dryer on the “air fluff” setting, then hung it up to air-dry. It’s heavy and large, so I ended up draping it over a drying rack and a (turned off) radiator. It did take over 24 hours to feel completely dry, but I was relieved that it remained just as soft and silky as when it first arrived. (The whole process was very similar to Druckman’s experience washing the Lola.)

The main drawback of the Cocoon is the high price. When friends have asked about it, I’ve felt shy about recommending it simply because it’s so expensive. At full price, the Cocoon blanket is actually a bit cheaper than the Lola blanket, but it’s easier to get the Lola at a discount because the brand runs frequent sales and often gives promo codes to influencers. And there are plenty of considerably cheaper faux-fur throw options out there — Brooklinen’s is $129 (but currently on sale for $97), and Anthropologie’s is under $100. Now that I’ve tried the Cocoon and grown to love it, however, I think it’s worth the splurge if you are a true plush-blanket aficionado. I also think it would make for a really luxe gift for someone who wouldn’t typically buy it for themself.

entry.summary: From kid ceramics to T-shirts.
entry.content:
What do you do with the gifted tchotchkes, the ticket stubs, the old journals from elementary school, the years and years of kid art? Sentimental clutter is a type of mess that is “radioactive, delightful, too immersive to approach,” as one respondent describes it — it symbolizes something you love, so you can’t just throw it away. Attempt to organize it and you’ll get sucked into a nostalgia vortex, and it’s immune to the pragmatic calculus of clearing out a junk drawer or medicine cabinet.

The first step with sentimental clutter is to acknowledge what it means to you. If these objects are sacred, treat them as such. These are items in your archive; if there were a museum exhibition about your life, they’d be on display. Keep anything in circulation that can still be useful — use that art-class pinch pot to store your keys! — but if the function is purely sentimental, find a place to store them that is safe and accessible. Below are my solutions for four different sentimental-clutter puzzles.

Primary complaint: “My 8-year-old has been taking a weekly pottery class for three years and has amassed more kiln-fired work than I can handle. This is the top of the buffet in our dining room, and there’s also a big storage tub of things wrapped in newspaper and labeled with the year she made it. We need some sort of display situation that I have not hit on yet.”

What a fantastic collection. The first thing I‘d say is to find a purpose for anything functional — use the trays and coil pots to store jewelry, hairpins, salt in the kitchen, et cetera. Then reclaim some buffet real estate by arranging things vertically. One quick way to do this is to prop up anything flat on a display stand. I’ve linked three options below, ranging from less to more robust — acrylic for smaller pieces, wood and metal wire for the heavier stuff.

You can also build upward with a tiered tray. I’m assuming a kid curator might be making adjustments to the display, so I’d recommend something with a lip to avoid ceramics tumbling off. Cupcake stands are about the right dimensions and usually have a shallow lip.

If there’s space for it, a corner shelf could serve as an extra display area for larger pieces. I love the spindle detail on this one; it could hold a few prized items that rotate in and out and looks adult enough to adapt to changing uses.

Primary complaint: “I have two bins of childhood journals that have been stressing me out for years. They definitely smell a little musty; I have a finished basement, but turns out it’s still a basement. I’d like them to be properly stored, but I don’t need them organized because I’d rather not have to go through everything.”

I have the exact solution to this problem — weathertight storage bins from the Container Store. Before testing them myself, they were recommended by a professional organizer who described them as “by far one of the most durable on the market.” The lid has a foam seal that keeps air and moisture out. While working on this article, I walked up to the attic and cracked open my weathertight bin full of mementos for the first time in years to give it a sniff. No mustiness at all.

When storing things that feel too emotionally charged to open in the moment, labeling helps — it lowers the psychological barrier when you do finally feel like diving in. An unlabeled storage bin is a jack-in-the-box where something can pop out and surprise you; the label gives you some degree of control over what you’re getting into.

Primary complaint: “I have several boxes and folders of crap; I can never throw a letter or card away. The worst, though, is the T-shirts. The right side is what I call my ‘couldn’t possibly’ pile where I don’t even wear them to sleep but they have sentimental value. A book would be cool; I don’t want a quilt, and I don’t really want them on my wall.”

I really puzzled over this one — how can you get T-shirts into a book without requiring a ton of work to mount each one individually? I was on a wild goose chase looking at XXL scrapbooks when I stumbled on the archival boxes below, which have the thick spine of a three-ring binder and the closed sides of a box. If you fold up the T-shirts and use binder clips to connect them to the metal spine, you end up with a booklike storage solution with the T-shirts as the “pages.”

Here’s a pack of binder clips to attach the T-shirts to the central rings (you only need to use one side of the clip; pinch the other to remove it). If you want to get really crafty, you can use a corrugated board to stiffen each T-shirt. I’ve linked an archival one below, but an old cardboard box would work as well.

One respondent sent in an account of her collections across a range of “clutterboxes,” which contain earrings, Arctic fox teeth, worry dolls, “random chunks of amber,” and owl feathers. To me, this is a perfect solution: giving each tiny collection a special home.

The containers are “mainly inherited from my tchotchke-loving mother,” but they also recommended Etsy as a good source. Below are some clutterboxes to house your collections; try searching for “pewter box,” “Bakelite box,” and “trinket box.”
